rows.notes: The study is a conceptual/policy perspective paper (HESS Anthropocene special issue) comparing three basins through illustrative case narratives built from secondary census and statistical data (Table 1, Figs. 5-6) and cited literature (AEVAL 2010, L<U+00F3>pez-Gunn et al. 2012 for Guadiana water savings reuse; Vicu<U+00F1>a et al. for climate; Bauer 2004 for water rights). It reports no experiment, survey or model run of its own. It does describe the rebound/efficiency paradox for drip in Limar<U+00ED> (drip rising to 60% of area while irrigated area rose from ~40,000 to >60,000 ha, with subsidies conditional on area extension) and for Guadiana, which matches the claim narratively, but this is a descriptive co-occurrence from official statistics and others' results, not the study's own result. Only original quantitative element is Fig. 3 (streamflow vs precipitation exceedance frequencies), which the authors state cannot be used to infer conditions before efficiency changes. Doubt: a reader could treat the compiled-statistics case analysis as primary; answered no per rule.

Same reason: conceptual/policy synthesis with case illustrations, not a primary study. On the specific claim (flood-to-drip conversion reduces return flows supporting ecosystems), the paper asserts the scale paradox conceptually and shows low outlet streamflow in Limar<U+00ED> (Fig. 3, 5 m3/s threshold exceeded 35% of time downstream vs 65% upstream) but explicitly states the records do not allow inference of the situation before the increase in irrigated area and efficiency, only a conjecture. Imperial Valley ecosystem impacts (Salton Sea, cross-border seepage) relate to canal lining, sprinkler and transfers rather than drip (would be a technology mismatch if taken as evidence); Guadiana environmental impacts are attributed to cited work (Blanco-Guti<U+00E9>rrez et al. 2011, 2013). No own measured result on drip versus flood return flows.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper is a perspective/conceptual comparison of three basins (Limar<U+00ED>, Imperial Valley, Guadiana) using official statistics and literature; it defines efficiency, scale and sectoral paradoxes and illustrates them narratively. Its only original data analysis is the Limar<U+00ED> streamflow-precipitation comparison (Fig. 3), which the authors acknowledge cannot establish change over time. Treated as non-primary; if a rater considers it primary, both claims would still lack an own measured result attributable to drip specifically.
